findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Evaluate adding a bounded cancel+await to the opcert lifespan (mirroring review_bot/app.py:155-160's wait_for(gather(...), shutdown_cancel_seconds()) with straggler abandonment) as a complementary defense, so shutdown cannot hang unboundedly regardless of the wait_for fix, and record why it was or was not adopted.
evidence: src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py:55-59 awaits `await task` with no timeout after task.cancel()
src/rebar/review_bot/app.py:155-160 bounds the identical cancel+await under shutdown_cancel_seconds() and abandons pending tasks (c2ba)

Plan text: 'sweep other asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(...)) lifecycle sites and parallel app surfaces for the confirmed pattern' — the sibling already implements the bounded-await defense the plan does not adopt
findings.finding: The plan repairs the worker's wait_for cancellation semantics but leaves the opcert lifespan's `await task` unbounded (app.py:55-59), unlike the sibling review_bot lifespan which bounds cancel+await with wait_for(gather(...), shutdown_cancel_seconds()) and abandons stragglers (app.py:155-160, commit c2ba). A complementary bounded-await defense would make shutdown robust regardless of any slow-to-cancel cause and align the two parallel app surfaces the plan already sweeps.
findings.location: Phase 2 plan, 'Repair the cancellation mechanism in src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py'
scenarios: Any future slow-to-cancel condition in the worker (shielded region, synchronous finally, a different asyncio bug) reintroduces the identical unbounded shutdown hang
Divergence between opcert and review_bot lifespan shutdown discipline makes the two parallel surfaces behave differently under the same cancellation collision
findings.suggested_fix: In the plan's repair step, additionally bound the lifespan finalizer's `await task` under a shutdown-cancel timeout and abandon still-pending tasks, matching the sibling review_bot lifespan pattern; treat the wait_for-semantics fix and the bounded-await as layered defenses.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State a repeat/iteration budget for the xdist and lone-test reproduction ACs (e.g. run the repro N times / under stress) so an intermittent hang is proven absent, not merely absent in one run.
evidence: Problem: 'Python 3.11 CI intermittently kills an xdist worker'
Proven mechanism: the deterministic harness 'made the original reproduction pass 20/20' — the fix proof used a repeat count, but the xdist repro AC states none
An intermittent hang that passes once cannot be distinguished from a genuine fix without a repeat/stress iteration count
findings.finding: The AC 'The original lone-test and xdist reproductions no longer hang on Python 3.11' proves a non-hang for an INTERMITTENT failure (the problem statement says only 'three recent runs' hit the 300s guard) with no stated repeat count or iteration budget, so a single green run does not distinguish a fixed bug from a lucky pass.
findings.location: Acceptance criteria: 'The original lone-test and xdist reproductions no longer hang on Python 3.11.'
scenarios: A single xdist run passes by chance; the fix is later found insufficient because the race window narrowed but was not closed
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the AC: run the lone-test and xdist reproduction under Python 3.11 for a stated iteration count (mirroring the harness's 20/20) and require zero hangs across all iterations.

evidence: 2 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State which established remediation the fix adopts (e.g. asyncio.timeout() available in 3.11, or the CPython GH-98607 pattern) and justify any bespoke reimplementation against it.
evidence: Plan text: 'replacing only wait_for with Python 3.12-style timeout semantics made the original reproduction pass 20/20' and 'Repair the cancellation mechanism ... while preserving ... Python 3.12+ behavior'
Web (docs.python.org asyncio-task): 'asyncio.timeout(delay) ... Added in version 3.11' — a cancellation-safe context manager available on the affected 3.11 runtime
Web (github.com/python/cpython issue 86296 + GH-98607): the wait_for swallowed-cancellation bug and its upstream fix are documented prior art the repair could mirror
Reinventing an in-repo 'timeout semantics' shim when a stdlib primitive (asyncio.timeout) or the upstream fix already solves this is the anti-repackaging check
findings.finding: The plan commits to a bespoke 'Python 3.12-style timeout semantics' reimplementation of wait_for without considering established prior-art remediations for CPython issue 86296 — notably asyncio.timeout() (a cancellation-safe context manager available in Python 3.11 since 3.11.0) or the upstream CPython GH-98607 fix pattern.
findings.location: Phase 2 plan, bullet 3: 'Repair the cancellation mechanism in src/rebar/opcert_service/app.py'
scenarios: Reviewer/implementer picks a hand-rolled wrapper that reintroduces a subtler cancellation race that asyncio.timeout already handles
Future maintainers cannot tell whether the bespoke code is intentional vs an unaware reimplementation
findings.suggested_fix: In the Phase 2 repair bullet, name the concrete mechanism — prefer stdlib asyncio.timeout() (3.11+) over a hand-rolled shim, and if a bespoke approach is chosen, record why asyncio.timeout()/the upstream GH-98607 fix is insufficient.
